'''''Eucalyptus deglupta''''', commonly known as the '''rainbow eucalyptus''',<ref name="SelecTree">{{Cite web|url=https://selectree.calpoly.edu/tree-detail/eucalyptus-deglupta|publisher=California Polytechnic State University |website=SelecTree: A Tree Selection Guide|title=''Eucalyptus deglupta''|language=en|access-date=2018-04-29}}</ref> '''Mindanao gum''', or '''rainbow gum''',<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.nparks.gov.sg/florafaunaweb/flora/2/8/2886 |title= Eucalyptus deglupta (Rainbow Gum) |author= <!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.-->
|publisher= nparks.gov.sg |access-date=December 9, 2025 |url-status=live
|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20251209173253/https://www.nparks.gov.sg/florafaunaweb/flora/2/8/2886 |archive-date=December 9, 2025 }}</ref> is a species of tall tree native to the [[Philippines]], [[Indonesia]] and [[Papua New Guinea]]. It is the only ''[[Eucalyptus]]'' species that usually lives in rainforest, with a natural range that extends into the Northern Hemisphere. It is characterized by multi-coloured bark.

==Description==
''Eucalyptus deglupta'' is a fast-growing tree that typically reaches a height of {{cvt|60-78|m}},<ref>{{cite book | last= Womersley | first= John S. | date= 1978 |title= Handbook of the Flora of Papua New Guinea | location= Melbourne | publisher= Melbourne University Press | page= <not recorded>}}</ref> with the trunk up to {{cvt|240|cm|0}} in diameter and with [[Buttress root|buttresses]] up to {{cvt|4|m}} high. It has smooth, orange-tinted bark that sheds in strips, revealing streaks of pale green, red, orange, grey, and purplish brown. The branchlets are roughly square in cross section, often with narrow wings on the corners. The leaves are arranged in opposite pairs, mostly {{cvt|75-150|mm|0}} long and {{cvt|50-75|mm|0}} wide on a short [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]]. The flower buds are arranged in a branching [[inflorescence]] in leaf [[wikt:axil|axil]]s, or on the end of branchlets, each branch with groups of seven buds, the individual buds on a [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]] about {{cvt|5|mm|frac=16}} long. Mature buds are pale green or cream-coloured, roughly spherical in shape and {{cvt|2-5|mm|frac=16}} in diameter with a hemispherical [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]] with a small point on the top. Flowering time depends on location, and the [[stamen]]s that give the flowers their colour are white and pale yellow. The fruit is a woody, brown, hemispherical [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] about {{cvt|3-5|mm|frac=16}} long and wide, with three or four valves extending beyond the rim of the fruit. Each cell of the fruit contains between three and twelve minute brown seeds, each with a small wing.<ref name="Forestry">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus deglupta'' |url=https://www.worldagroforestry.org/treedb/AFTPDFS/Eucalyptus_deglupta.PDF |publisher=World of Forestry |access-date=28 May 2019}}</ref><ref name="Missouri">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus deglupta'' |url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=282890 |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden |access-date=28 May 2019}}</ref>

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Eucalyptus deglupta'' was first formally described in 1850 by [[Carl Ludwig Blume]] who published the description in his book ''Museum Botanicum Lugduno-Batavum sive stirpium Exoticarum, Novarum vel Minus Cognitarum ex Vivis aut Siccis Brevis Expositio et Descriptio'' from material collected in mountain forests in [[Sulawesi|the Celebes]].<ref name="POWO" /><ref name="Blume">{{cite book |last1=Blume |first1=Carl Ludwig |title=Museum Botanicum Lugduno-Batavum sive stirpium Exoticarum, Novarum vel Minus Cognitarum ex Vivis aut Siccis Brevis Expositio et Descriptio |date=1850 |pages=83–84 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/192635#page/95/mode/1up |access-date=28 May 2019}}</ref> The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''deglupta'') is a [[Latin]] word meaning "peeled off, husked or shelled".<ref name="RWB">{{cite book|author-link1=Roland W. Brown|last1=Brown|first1=Roland Wilbur|title=The Composition of Scientific Words|date=1956|publisher=Smithsonian Institution Press|location=Washington, D.C.|page=716}}</ref>

In 1914, [[Adolph Daniel Edward Elmer]] described ''Eugenia binacag'' in ''Leaflets of Philippine Botany'', the [[Binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''binacag'' a local name for the tree,<ref name="Elmer1">{{cite journal |last1=Elmer |first1=Adolph D.E. |title=Myrtaceae from Mount Urdaneta |journal=Leaflets of Philippine Botany |date=1914 |volume=7 |pages=2351–2352 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/6766#page/34/mode/1up |access-date=9 October 2020}}</ref> but in 1915 changed the name to ''Eucalyptus binacag''.<ref name="Elmer2">{{cite journal |last1=Elmer |first1=Adolph D.E. |title=Two Hundred Twenty Six New Species - II |journal=Leaflets of Philippine Botany |date=1915 |volume=8 |page=2776 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/6767#page/60/mode/1up |access-date=9 October 2020}}</ref> However, the species had already been named ''E. deglupta'' by [[Carl Ludwig Blume|Blume]] in 1850 and ''E. binacag'' is now regarded as a [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]].<ref name="POWO" />

In 1854, [[Asa Gray]] described ''Eucalyptus multiflora'' in ''[[United States Exploring Expedition]] - Botany, Phanerogamia'' from an unpublished description by [[Louis Claude Richard]],<ref name="POWO1">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus multiflora'' |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:593148-1 |publisher=Plants of the World Online |access-date=14 November 2022}}</ref><ref name="A.Gray">{{cite book |last1=Gray |first1=Asa |title=United States Exploring Expedition - Botany, Phanerogramia, Part 1 |date=1854 |publisher=C. Sherman |location=Philadelphia |pages=554–555 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/40382252#page/559/mode/1up |access-date=10 October 2020}}</ref> but is a [[nomen illegitimum]] because the name was already in use for a different species (''Eucalyptus multiflora'' <small>[[Poir.]]</small>) now known as ''[[Eucalyptus robusta]]''.<ref name=APC>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus robusta''|url= https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/58105|publisher=Australian Plant Census|access-date=10 October 2020}}</ref>

''Eucalyptus sarassa'' and ''E. versicolor'', first described in 1850 by Blume in his book ''Museum botanicum Lugduno-Batavum'',<ref name="Blume1">{{cite book |last1=Blume |first1=Carl Ludwig |title=Museum botanicum Lugduno-Batavum |date=1850 |publisher=E.J. Brill |location=New York |page=84 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/192635#page/96/mode/1up |access-date=10 October 2020}}</ref> and ''E. schlechteri'' first described by [[Ludwig Diels]] in [[Adolf Engler]]'s book ''Botanische Jahrbücher für Systematik, Pflanzengeschichte und Pflanzengeographie''<ref name="Diels">{{cite book |last1=Diels |first1=Ludwig |editor-last1=Engler |editor-first1=Adolf |title=Botanische Jahrbücher für Systematik, Pflanzengeschichte und Pflanzengeographie |date=1922 |publisher=Wilhelm Engelmann |location=Leipzig |page=423 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/720#page/430/mode/1up |access-date=10 October 2020}}</ref> are also considered to be synonyms of ''E. deglupta'' by [[Plants of the World Online]].<ref name="POWO" />

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Eucalyptus deglupta Blume (Maui).jpg|thumb|''Eucalyptus deglupta'' Blume, [[Maui]]]]The rainbow eucalyptus grows in lowland and lower montane rainforest from sea level to elevations of up to {{cvt|1800|m}}. It is native to the Philippines, Indonesia, and Papua New Guinea, but has been widely planted in many other countries.<ref name="POWO" />

The populations of this species are severely fragmented in the wild and the overall population is decreasing. Over the last 210 years it is estimated that there has been a 30% decline of the overall population. The [[International Union for the Conservation of Nature]] listed ''E.{{nbsp}}deglupta'' as a [[vulnerable species]] in 2019.<ref name="iucn status 21 June 2019"/>

==Uses==
===Pulpwood===
This tree is grown widely around the world in tree [[plantation]]s, mainly for [[pulpwood]] used in making white paper. It is the dominant species used for pulpwood plantations in the [[Philippines]].<ref>{{cite web|publisher=National Resources Institute|title=Notes on Eucalyptus|url=http://www.nri.org/biomass/conference_papers/notes_on_eucalypts.pdf|access-date=2007-01-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927191726/http://www.nri.org/biomass/conference_papers/notes_on_eucalypts.pdf|archive-date=2007-09-27}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Carroll |first1=Jackie |title=Eucalyptus |url=https://www.gardeningknowhow.com/ornamental/trees/eucalyptus/rainbow-eucalyptus-tree.htm |website=Gardening Know How |date=20 April 2015 }}</ref>

===Use in horticulture===
[[File:Rainbow Eucalyptus Maui.jpg|thumb|right|Bark of ''E. deglupta'' in a grove of trees on [[Maui]], Hawaii]]''Eucalyptus deglupta'' is commonly planted as an ornamental tree in frost-free climates such as Hawaii, Southern California, Texas and Florida.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gardeningknowhow.com/ornamental/trees/eucalyptus/rainbow-eucalyptus-tree.htm|title=Rainbow Eucalyptus Tree – Learn About Rainbow Eucalyptus Growing Conditions|website=www.gardeningknowhow.com|date=20 April 2015 |language=en-US|access-date=2018-04-29}}</ref> It is planted in at least three locations in coastal Los Angeles County, including Santa Monica and San Marino at the Huntington Botanical Garden. These trees were still growing, but relatively young at approximately 30–40 years in 1988, at the UCLA Botanic Garden and as a LA City street tree.<ref name="Hodel">{{cite book |last1=Hodel |first1=Donald R. |title=Exceptional trees of Los Angeles |date=1988 |publisher=California Arboretum Foundation |location=Arcadia, California |isbn=0-9621121-0-0 |page=31 |edition=1st}}</ref>

If grown from seed, the temperature should be around {{convert|68|-|72|F|disp=flip}}.<ref name="SFGate">{{cite web |url=https://homeguides.sfgate.com/germination-eucalyptus-deglupta-22711.html |title=Germination of a ''Eucalyptus Deglupta'' |last=Caines |first=Kimberley |website=SFGate |access-date=2019-10-31 }}</ref> Plants can be grown from cuttings of trees younger than 5 years old. Once a tree reaches 5 years of age, root inhibition prevents the generation of roots from cuttings.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Davidson|first=John|date=1973|title=Reproduction of ''Eucalyptus deglupt''a by cuttings|url=https://www.scionresearch.com/__data/assets/pdf_file/0007/30967/NZJFS421974DAVIDSON191_203.pdf|journal=New Zealand Journal of Forestry Science|volume=4|pages=191–204}}</ref> It thrives in rich medium-to-wet soil in full sun and is intolerant of frost.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=282890|title=''Eucalyptus deglupta'' - Plant Finder|website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org|language=en-US|access-date=2018-04-29}}</ref> In botanical gardens such as [[Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden]] in Florida, the tree does show the intense colour range as seen in the tree's normal range.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://eucalyptusdeglupta.com/rainbowarticle.pdf|title=Under the Rainbow|last=Garner|first=LariAnn|access-date=2007-01-10}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=M3e5wyFJY-8C&pg=PA228|title=Nature's palette: the science of plant color|author=David Webster Lee|publisher=University of Chicago Press|year=2007|isbn=978-0-226-47105-1|page=228|access-date=2011-04-22}}</ref>
